title: Lecture 9: Agile Development Methods and Practices
summary: This lecture provides a comprehensive overview of agile software development methodologies, exploring the Agile Manifesto, Scrum framework, Extreme Programming practices, and iterative development approaches. Students will understand how agile techniques integrate with software engineering principles and learn to apply basic agile development techniques in real-world contexts.
learningObjectives: Understand the core values and principles of the Agile Manifesto and their impact on modern software development
Apply the Scrum framework including roles, artifacts, and ceremonies to organize software projects
Implement Extreme Programming (XP) practices to improve code quality and team collaboration
Design and execute iterative and incremental development cycles
Create effective user stories and conduct sprint planning sessions
Compare and contrast agile versus traditional development approaches and select appropriate methodologies for different contexts

sections.title: Introduction to Agile Software Development
learningGoals: Understand the historical context that led to agile methodologies
Recognize the limitations of traditional waterfall approaches
Appreciate the paradigm shift agile represents in software engineering

subsections.title: The Evolution from Traditional to Agile
keyPoints: Traditional waterfall model: sequential phases with limited flexibility
Challenges in traditional approaches: late feedback, rigid requirements, long delivery cycles
The software crisis of the 1990s and need for adaptive methodologies
Emergence of lightweight methodologies in the late 1990s
examples: Case study: Failed waterfall project due to changing requirements
Comparison timeline: 18-month waterfall vs. 2-week agile iterations
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Timeline showing evolution from waterfall (1970s) through iterative models to agile (2001-present)

subsections.title: The Agile Manifesto: Values and Principles
keyPoints: Four core values: Individuals over processes, working software over documentation, customer collaboration over contracts, responding to change over following plans
Twelve principles underlying agile development
Emphasis on continuous delivery, sustainable development, and technical excellence
The balance: valuing items on the right while valuing items on the left more
examples: Real-world interpretation: How 'working software over documentation' doesn't mean no documentation
Customer collaboration example: Daily standup with product owner vs. quarterly review meetings
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Visual representation of the four Agile Manifesto values with concrete examples for each

exercises: Group discussion: Identify a software project scenario and determine which agile values would be most critical
Reflection: Map traditional software engineering practices from earlier lectures to agile principles

sections.title: The Scrum Framework
learningGoals: Master the three roles, three artifacts, and five ceremonies of Scrum
Understand how Scrum implements agile principles in practice
Apply Scrum framework to organize a software development project

subsections.title: Scrum Roles and Responsibilities
keyPoints: Product Owner: Maximizes product value, manages product backlog, represents stakeholders
Scrum Master: Facilitates process, removes impediments, coaches team on Scrum practices
Development Team: Self-organizing, cross-functional, 3-9 members, collectively responsible
Role boundaries and collaboration patterns
Common anti-patterns: Product Owner as project manager, Scrum Master as team lead
examples: Product Owner prioritizing features based on business value and technical dependencies
Scrum Master facilitating conflict resolution without dictating solutions
Development team self-organizing to tackle a complex technical challenge
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Scrum team structure showing three roles and their interactions with arrows indicating communication flows

subsections.title: Scrum Artifacts
keyPoints: Product Backlog: Ordered list of everything needed in the product, single source of requirements
Sprint Backlog: Selected product backlog items plus plan for delivering increment
Increment: Sum of all completed backlog items, must be in usable condition
Definition of Done: Shared understanding of what 'complete' means
Transparency through artifacts: everyone sees the same information
examples: Sample product backlog with user stories ordered by priority and estimated
Sprint backlog showing tasks broken down from user stories with daily updates
Definition of Done checklist: code reviewed, tests passing, documentation updated, deployed to staging
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Flow diagram showing how items move from Product Backlog to Sprint Backlog to Increment

subsections.title: Scrum Ceremonies and Events
keyPoints: Sprint: Time-boxed iteration (1-4 weeks), consistent duration, creates rhythm
Sprint Planning: Team selects work and creates sprint goal (max 8 hours for 1-month sprint)
Daily Scrum: 15-minute synchronization, three questions format, identify impediments
Sprint Review: Inspect increment, adapt product backlog, stakeholder collaboration (max 4 hours)
Sprint Retrospective: Team inspects itself, creates improvement plan (max 3 hours)
Time-boxing principle: all events have maximum durations
examples: Sprint Planning agenda: Part 1 (What can be done?) and Part 2 (How will it be done?)
Daily Scrum in practice: What I did yesterday, what I'll do today, any blockers
Retrospective techniques: Start-Stop-Continue, Sailboat, 4Ls (Liked, Learned, Lacked, Longed for)
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Sprint cycle diagram showing all ceremonies positioned within a 2-week sprint timeline

exercises: Role-play exercise: Conduct a 10-minute sprint planning session for a simple project
Create a sample product backlog with 10 user stories for a mobile app, ordered by priority
Design a Definition of Done appropriate for a web application project

sections.title: Extreme Programming (XP) Practices
learningGoals: Understand XP values and their relationship to code quality
Apply core XP practices to improve software construction
Integrate XP techniques with object-oriented programming principles

subsections.title: XP Values and Core Practices
keyPoints: Five values: Communication, Simplicity, Feedback, Courage, Respect
Pair Programming: Two programmers, one keyboard, continuous code review
Test-Driven Development (TDD): Write test first, then code to pass test, then refactor
Continuous Integration: Integrate code multiple times daily, automated builds
Collective Code Ownership: Anyone can modify any code, shared responsibility
Simple Design: Do the simplest thing that could possibly work, YAGNI principle
examples: TDD cycle: Red (failing test) → Green (passing code) → Refactor (improve design)
Pair programming roles: Driver (typing) and Navigator (reviewing, thinking ahead)
Simple design example: Avoiding premature optimization and over-engineering
subsections.suggestedDiagram: TDD cycle diagram showing the red-green-refactor loop with code examples at each stage

subsections.title: Additional XP Practices and Integration
keyPoints: Refactoring: Continuous improvement of code structure without changing behavior
Coding Standards: Team agrees on conventions for consistency
Sustainable Pace: 40-hour weeks, no overtime as standard practice
Small Releases: Frequent delivery of working software to production
On-site Customer: Customer representative available for questions
Integration with Design by Contract: XP testing complements DbC assertions
examples: Refactoring catalog: Extract Method, Rename Variable, Introduce Parameter Object
Coding standards document: Naming conventions, formatting rules, comment guidelines
Small release strategy: Deploy to production every two weeks vs. quarterly
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Mind map showing how XP practices reinforce each other (e.g., TDD enables refactoring, CI requires collective ownership)

exercises: Practice TDD: Write tests first for a simple function (e.g., string validator), then implement
Pair programming simulation: Two students solve a coding problem together, switching roles every 5 minutes
Refactoring exercise: Identify code smells in provided code and apply appropriate refactorings

sections.title: Iterative and Incremental Development
learningGoals: Distinguish between iterative and incremental approaches
Plan effective iteration cycles
Manage technical debt and architecture evolution across iterations

subsections.title: Iteration Planning and Execution
keyPoints: Iterative: Refining and improving through repeated cycles
Incremental: Building piece by piece, adding functionality
Combining both: Each iteration adds features and refines existing ones
Iteration length: Typically 1-4 weeks, consistent duration preferred
Velocity: Measure of work completed per iteration, used for planning
Burndown charts: Visual tracking of remaining work
examples: Incremental example: Building e-commerce site—iteration 1: product catalog, iteration 2: shopping cart, iteration 3: checkout
Iterative example: Refining user interface based on feedback each iteration
Velocity calculation: Team completes 25 story points in iteration 1, 28 in iteration 2, average velocity = 26.5
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Comparison chart showing waterfall (sequential phases) vs. iterative-incremental (overlapping cycles with growing functionality)

subsections.title: Managing Evolution and Technical Debt
keyPoints: Technical debt: Shortcuts taken for speed that require future rework
Architectural runway: Preparing infrastructure for upcoming features
Refactoring as debt repayment: Allocating time each iteration
Balancing new features with quality improvements
Emergent architecture: Design evolves based on actual needs, not predicted needs
Spike solutions: Time-boxed research to reduce uncertainty
examples: Technical debt example: Hard-coding configuration for quick demo, must refactor to configuration file later
Spike: 2-day investigation into database scalability options before committing to architecture
Refactoring budget: Reserve 20% of each sprint for technical debt reduction
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Graph showing feature delivery vs. technical debt over iterations, illustrating sustainable vs. unsustainable pace

exercises: Planning exercise: Given a project description, divide it into 4 iterations with clear increments
Calculate velocity and forecast completion: Given past iteration data, predict when 100 story points will be complete
Identify technical debt in a code sample and propose a refactoring schedule

sections.title: User Stories and Sprint Planning
learningGoals: Write effective user stories following INVEST criteria
Estimate user stories using relative sizing techniques
Conduct productive sprint planning sessions

subsections.title: Writing and Estimating User Stories
keyPoints: User story format: As a [role], I want [feature], so that [benefit]
INVEST criteria: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable
Acceptance criteria: Specific conditions that must be met for story to be complete
Story points vs. hours: Relative sizing vs. absolute time estimates
Planning poker: Team-based estimation technique using Fibonacci sequence
Epic stories: Large stories that must be broken down into smaller ones
examples: Good user story: 'As a customer, I want to filter products by price range, so that I can find items within my budget'
Acceptance criteria: 'Given a product list, when I set min price to $10 and max to $50, then only products in that range are displayed'
Planning poker session: Team estimates story, reveals cards simultaneously, discusses outliers, re-estimates
subsections.suggestedDiagram: User story card template showing story format, acceptance criteria, story points, and notes sections

subsections.title: Sprint Planning Process
keyPoints: Input: Prioritized product backlog, team velocity, team capacity
Output: Sprint goal, sprint backlog, commitment
Part 1 - What: Product Owner presents top priorities, team asks questions, team selects stories
Part 2 - How: Team breaks stories into tasks, identifies dependencies, creates plan
Capacity planning: Account for holidays, training, support work
Sprint goal: Cohesive objective that provides focus beyond individual stories
examples: Sprint goal example: 'Enable users to manage their account settings'
Capacity calculation: 5 team members × 8 hours/day × 10 days = 400 hours - 50 hours (meetings, support) = 350 available hours
Task breakdown: User story 'User login' → Tasks: Design login UI (4h), Implement authentication (8h), Write tests (4h), Update documentation (2h)
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Sprint planning flow chart showing inputs, two-part process, and outputs with decision points

exercises: Write 5 user stories for a library management system following INVEST criteria
Conduct planning poker: Estimate provided user stories as a team
Sprint planning simulation: Given a product backlog and team velocity, select stories for next sprint and create sprint goal

sections.title: Agile vs. Traditional Development Approaches
learningGoals: Compare agile and traditional methodologies across multiple dimensions
Select appropriate methodology based on project context
Understand hybrid approaches and when to use them

subsections.title: Comparative Analysis
keyPoints: Requirements: Agile (emergent, evolving) vs. Traditional (defined upfront, frozen)
Planning: Agile (adaptive, rolling wave) vs. Traditional (comprehensive, upfront)
Control: Agile (empirical, inspect-adapt) vs. Traditional (defined process, variance control)
Customer involvement: Agile (continuous collaboration) vs. Traditional (milestone reviews)
Risk management: Agile (early, frequent delivery) vs. Traditional (risk analysis phase)
Team structure: Agile (self-organizing, cross-functional) vs. Traditional (specialized roles, hierarchy)
Documentation: Agile (just enough, working software) vs. Traditional (comprehensive, contractual)
examples: Requirements evolution: Agile project pivots based on user feedback after iteration 3; waterfall project requires formal change request
Risk mitigation: Agile delivers core feature in iteration 1 to validate assumptions; waterfall completes all design before coding
Team dynamics: Agile team decides how to implement feature; traditional team follows detailed design specification
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Comparison table with dimensions (requirements, planning, control, etc.) showing agile vs. traditional characteristics

subsections.title: Selecting and Adapting Methodologies
keyPoints: Project suitability factors: Requirements stability, team size, criticality, organizational culture
Agile works well: Innovative products, changing requirements, small-medium teams, low criticality
Traditional works well: Stable requirements, large teams, safety-critical systems, regulatory compliance
Hybrid approaches: Combining elements (e.g., agile development with waterfall project management)
Scaling agile: SAFe, LeSS, Scrum of Scrums for large organizations
Tailoring: Adapting methodology to organizational context, not following dogmatically
examples: Hybrid example: Medical device software using waterfall for regulatory documentation but agile for development iterations
Unsuitable for pure agile: Air traffic control system with strict certification requirements
Scaling example: 10 Scrum teams working on same product using Scrum of Scrums for coordination
Tailoring example: Startup uses Scrum but skips Sprint Review because Product Owner is on team
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Decision tree for selecting methodology based on project characteristics (requirements clarity, team size, criticality)

exercises: Case analysis: Given 3 project scenarios, recommend agile, traditional, or hybrid approach with justification
Debate: Divide class into teams arguing for agile vs. traditional for a specific project type
Reflection: How do agile practices (ILO 6) integrate with object-oriented techniques (ILO 1-2) and Design by Contract (ILO 3) from earlier lectures?

sections.title: Integration with Software Engineering Principles
learningGoals: Connect agile practices to fundamental software engineering concepts
Apply agile techniques within object-oriented development
Understand how agile supports quality attributes

subsections.title: Agile and Software Quality
keyPoints: Quality built-in: TDD, continuous integration, pair programming prevent defects
Correctness: Automated tests verify behavior, acceptance criteria define correctness
Robustness: Frequent integration catches errors early, small increments limit blast radius
Extendibility: Refactoring maintains clean code, simple design enables change
Reusability: Collective ownership spreads knowledge, coding standards promote consistency
Connection to Design by Contract: Unit tests can verify preconditions, postconditions, invariants
examples: TDD supporting correctness: Tests document expected behavior and catch regressions
Refactoring for extendibility: Extract common code into reusable components each iteration
DbC integration: Eiffel assertions complement XP tests—assertions for internal correctness, tests for external behavior
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Mapping diagram showing how agile practices (TDD, refactoring, CI, etc.) support quality attributes (correctness, robustness, extendibility, reusability)

subsections.title: Agile in Object-Oriented Development
keyPoints: Iterative design: Classes and inheritance hierarchies emerge through refactoring
Design patterns in agile: Apply patterns when needed (YAGNI), refactor to patterns
Test-driven class design: Tests drive interface design, promote loose coupling
Continuous refactoring: Maintain SOLID principles throughout iterations
Agile architecture: Evolutionary design vs. big upfront design
Balance: Enough design to start, refactor as understanding grows
examples: Refactoring to Observer pattern: Start with simple notification, refactor to Observer when multiple listeners needed
TDD driving interface: Writing tests first leads to more testable, decoupled class designs
Evolutionary architecture: Start with simple layered architecture, introduce patterns as complexity warrants
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Iteration timeline showing how class design evolves: Iteration 1 (simple classes) → Iteration 2 (extract interfaces) → Iteration 3 (apply patterns) → Iteration 4 (refine hierarchy)

subsections.title: Practical Application and Summary
keyPoints: Agile as a mindset, not just practices: Embrace change, value individuals, focus on working software
Continuous improvement: Retrospectives drive process evolution
Metrics that matter: Velocity, burndown, cycle time, defect rates
Common pitfalls: Agile without discipline, skipping practices, cargo cult agile
Success factors: Team commitment, organizational support, customer collaboration
Future trends: DevOps, continuous delivery, agile at scale
examples: Retrospective improvement: Team identifies slow builds as impediment, invests in CI infrastructure
Pitfall example: Team does daily standups and sprints but skips TDD and refactoring—results in technical debt
Success story: Team reduces time-to-market from 6 months to 2 weeks through agile adoption
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Summary infographic showing agile ecosystem: Manifesto at center, surrounded by methodologies (Scrum, XP), practices, and benefits

exercises: Integration exercise: Design a 4-iteration plan for developing a class library using OO principles and agile practices
Reflection paper: How do agile techniques (ILO 6) complement other course topics (OO programming, design patterns, DbC)?
Case study analysis: Evaluate a real-world agile transformation story, identify success factors and challenges
